items.stem: Which of the following best describes "natural increase"?
options: Movement in which people have little or no choice, caused by conflict, persecution, disasters or development projects
The difference between births and deaths in a population, excluding migration, usually expressed per 1,000 or as a percentage
The number of males per 100 females in a population (or at birth)
A model showing how birth rates, death rates and population growth change through five stages as a country develops
items.answer: The difference between births and deaths in a population, excluding migration, usually expressed per 1,000 or as a percentage
items.markingKey: B. "natural increase" is the difference between births and deaths in a population, excluding migration, usually expressed per 1,000 or as a percentage.

items.stem: Briefly explain why death rates fall before birth rates in stage 2 of the demographic transition model.
items.answer: Improvements in food supply, clean water, sanitation and vaccination reduce mortality quickly, while high fertility persists because of cultural norms, the need for family labour and high infant mortality expectations.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Improvements in food supply, clean water, sanitation and vaccination reduce mortality quickly, while high fertility persists because of cultural norms, the need for family labour and high infant mortality expectations. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between stage 4 of the demographic transition model and stage 2.
items.answer: In stage 2 death rates fall rapidly while birth rates remain high, so growth is rapid; in stage 4 both rates are low and growth is slow or stable.
items.markingKey: In stage 2 death rates fall rapidly while birth rates remain high, so growth is rapid; in stage 4 both rates are low and growth is slow or stable. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Study the resource below.

Table: CBR and CDR (per 1,000) for four countries - Niger 44, 9; India 16, 7; Brazil 12, 7; Japan 6, 13.

Assign each country to a DTM stage, justifying with the data.
items.answer: Niger stage 2 (high CBR, low CDR); India late stage 3 (falling CBR); Brazil stage 3-4 (low rates, slow growth); Japan stage 5 (CDR > CBR).
items.markingKey: Niger stage 2 (high CBR, low CDR); India late stage 3 (falling CBR); Brazil stage 3-4 (low rates, slow growth); Japan stage 5 (CDR > CBR). Award 1 mark per valid point or correct step, up to [2]; data quoted must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

items.stem: With reference to Japan, explain how it illustrates stage 5 of the demographic transition model.
items.answer: The population has fallen since 2008, with deaths exceeding births by over 800,000 a year in recent years. Very low fertility and an elderly population cause natural decrease.
items.markingKey: Context (The population has fallen since 2008, with deaths exceeding births by over 800,000 a year in recent years.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Very low fertility and an elderly population cause natural decrease. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to stage 5 of the demographic transition model.

items.stem: The number of international migrants living in a Gulf city district was 38,713 people in 1990 and 42,947 people in 2010. Calculate (a) the percentage change and (b) the average annual compound rate of change over the 20 years.
items.markingKey: (a) M1 A1 +10.9%. (b) M1 (new/old)^(1/20) − 1, A1 +0.52% per year (simple average +0.55% earns M0 A0).

items.stem: Outline one argument for and one argument against the view that economic development is the main cause of fertility decline.
items.answer: Development helps, but female education, contraception access and policy often explain the timing and speed better.
items.markingKey: For: urbanisation and higher incomes raise the cost of children. Against: Bangladesh and Kerala show fertility can fall with low incomes through female education and family planning. [4]: 1 mark for a valid argument for, 1 for its development; 1 mark for a valid argument against, 1 for its development; generic points without geographical context are capped at 2.

items.stem: Examine the view that the demographic transition model is of limited use in explaining population change in today's low-income countries.
items.answer: The DTM remains a useful descriptive framework, but its timing and causes must be adapted to each country.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: based on 19th-century European experience; ignores migration and policy; some African fertility declines have stalled; HIV/AIDS raised death rates. Against / limitations: broad sequence (death rates then birth rates fall) has occurred almost everywhere; useful for predicting dependency and planning needs. A supported conclusion might be: The DTM remains a useful descriptive framework, but its timing and causes must be adapted to each country. items.stem: Briefly explain why total fertility rate is a better measure of fertility than the crude birth rate.
items.answer: TFR is not affected by the age structure of the population; CBR depends on how many women are of child-bearing age, so a youthful population may have a high CBR even if fertility per woman is falling.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: TFR is not affected by the age structure of the population; CBR depends on how many women are of child-bearing age, so a youthful population may have a high CBR even if fertility per woman is falling. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Every country must pass through the DTM stages at the same pace." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Pace varies widely: South Korea and Iran moved from high to low fertility within a generation, far faster than England.
items.markingKey: Pace varies widely: South Korea and Iran moved from high to low fertility within a generation, far faster than England. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Japan's population peaked in 2008 at about 128 million. Use the DTM to explain what has happened since.
items.answer: Japan has entered stage 5: very low fertility (TFR about 1.2) and an ageing population mean deaths exceed births, so the population has declined to about 124 million.
items.markingKey: Japan has entered stage 5: very low fertility (TFR about 1.2) and an ageing population mean deaths exceed births, so the population has declined to about 124 million.

items.stem: Estimates for Niger give a crude birth rate (CBR) of 44.2 per 1,000 and a crude death rate (CDR) of 8.2 per 1,000. The population is 220 million. (a) Calculate the NIR and the doubling time (rule of 70). (b) Assuming the NIR stays constant, project the population after 15 years. (c) Suggest one reason why the projection may be inaccurate.
items.answer: (a) 3.60%; ≈ 19 years (b) 220 × (1 + 0.0360)^15 ≈ 374.0 million (c) e.g. fertility decline as the country moves through the DTM, or migration is ignored.
items.markingKey: (a) A1 3.60%, A1 19 years. (b) M1 compound growth, A1 374.0 million (accept 373.8-374.2). (c) R1 valid reason, e.g. falling CBR, migration, mortality shocks.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A population with a large proportion of children under 15, typically giving a wide-based pyramid"?
items.answer: youthful population
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of youthful population.

items.stem: Explain why the dependency ratio is an imperfect measure of economic dependency.
items.answer: Many 15-64-year-olds are students, unemployed or carers, while many over-65s work and many children work in low-income countries; it ignores productivity and participation rates.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Many 15-64-year-olds are students, unemployed or carers, while many over-65s work and many children work in low-income countries; it ignores productivity and participation rates. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between old-age dependency and young dependency.
items.answer: Young dependency compares 0-14-year-olds with the working-age group and drives demand for schools; old-age dependency compares the 65+ group and drives pensions and elderly care.
items.markingKey: Young dependency compares 0-14-year-olds with the working-age group and drives demand for schools; old-age dependency compares the 65+ group and drives pensions and elderly care. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Suggest two policies that Japan could use to respond to its ageing population.
items.answer: Raising the pension age (e.g. encouraging work to 70), increasing immigration through the Specified Skilled Worker visa, using robotics and care technology, pro-natalist childcare support.
items.markingKey: Raising the pension age (e.g. encouraging work to 70), increasing immigration through the Specified Skilled Worker visa, using robotics and care technology, pro-natalist childcare support.

items.stem: The population of a peri-urban district of Dhaka was 842,276 people in 1995 and 1,609,718 people in 2015. Calculate the percentage change over the period.
items.markingKey: M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (1,609,718 − 842,276) ÷ 842,276 × 100; A1 +91.1% (sign or "increase/decrease" required).

items.stem: Examine the view that an ageing population is a greater challenge than a youthful population.
items.answer: Both are challenging; the scale depends on income, policy and timing - a youthful population with good investment offers more opportunity.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: rising pension and health costs with a shrinking workforce (Japan, Italy); difficult to reverse once fertility is very low. Against / limitations: youthful populations need schools, jobs and health services that poor countries struggle to provide; a youthful population can become a demographic dividend. A supported conclusion might be: Both are challenging; the scale depends on income, policy and timing - a youthful population with good investment offers more opportunity. items.stem: Which shape of pyramid indicates high birth rates and short life expectancy?
options: A wide base that narrows rapidly towards a narrow top
A bulge only in the 20-39 age group
A narrow base with a wide middle
items.answer: A wide base that narrows rapidly towards a narrow top
items.markingKey: A. This "triangular" shape typifies stage 2 countries such as Niger or Uganda.

items.stem: "An ageing population is a sign that a country is failing." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Ageing mainly reflects success - longer life expectancy and lower fertility - though it creates new challenges.
items.markingKey: Ageing mainly reflects success - longer life expectancy and lower fertility - though it creates new challenges. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Study the resource below.

Description of a population pyramid for the United Arab Emirates: very narrow bars for 0-19 and 50+, but very wide male bars for ages 25-44, where males outnumber females by about three to one.

Describe the pyramid.
items.answer: Dominated by working-age adults, especially men aged 25-44; few children and elderly; highly unbalanced sex ratio.
items.markingKey: Dominated by working-age adults, especially men aged 25-44; few children and elderly; highly unbalanced sex ratio. Award 1 mark per valid point or correct step, up to [3]; data quoted must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

items.answer: Indicative content: Named country with data (e.g. Japan 29% over 65 or Niger 49% under 15); economic, social and political consequences; responses; judgement.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Named country with data (e.g. Japan 29% over 65 or Niger 49% under 15); economic, social and political consequences; responses; judgement. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Movement in which people have little or no choice, caused by conflict, persecution, disasters or development projects"?
items.answer: forced migration
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of forced migration.

items.stem: Explain how a large refugee influx can affect a host country.
items.answer: Pressure on water, housing, schools and health care; competition for jobs and lower wages; environmental degradation around camps; but also labour supply, aid funding and new markets.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Pressure on water, housing, schools and health care; competition for jobs and lower wages; environmental degradation around camps; but also labour supply, aid funding and new markets. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "People displaced by climate disasters are legally refugees." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The 1951 Convention does not cover environmental displacement; most disaster-displaced people are IDPs within their own country.
items.markingKey: The 1951 Convention does not cover environmental displacement; most disaster-displaced people are IDPs within their own country. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: In one year Poland (population 37 million) received 80 thousand immigrants and lost 127 thousand emigrants. Calculate the net migration rate per 1,000 people.
items.answer: (80 − 127) thousand / 37 million × 1,000 = -1.3 per 1,000
items.markingKey: M1 immigrants − emigrants; A1 -1.3 per 1,000.

items.stem: The number of births registered in a province of Italy was 15,291 births in 1990 and 20,960 births in 2010. Calculate the percentage change over the period.
items.markingKey: M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (20,960 − 15,291) ÷ 15,291 × 100; A1 +37.1% (sign or "increase/decrease" required).

items.stem: Examine the causes and consequences of one forced migration you have studied.
items.answer: Indicative content: Named case (Rohingya, Syria, Ukraine, Sudan), causes (persecution, conflict), numbers, consequences for source and host areas and migrants; evaluation of responses.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Named case (Rohingya, Syria, Ukraine, Sudan), causes (persecution, conflict), numbers, consequences for source and host areas and migrants; evaluation of responses. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "forced migration"?
options: An informal term for a person displaced by environmental change or disaster, not recognised under the 1951 Convention
The principle of international law that refugees must not be returned to a country where they face serious threats to life or freedom
Movement in which people have little or no choice, caused by conflict, persecution, disasters or development projects
A population in which the proportion of older people (usually 65+) is increasing, raising the median age
items.answer: Movement in which people have little or no choice, caused by conflict, persecution, disasters or development projects
items.markingKey: C. "forced migration" is movement in which people have little or no choice, caused by conflict, persecution, disasters or development projects.

items.stem: Explain the difference between an economic migrant and a refugee.
items.answer: A refugee is forced to flee persecution or conflict and cannot safely return; an economic migrant chooses to move to improve income or opportunities and can usually return home.
items.markingKey: A refugee is forced to flee persecution or conflict and cannot safely return; an economic migrant chooses to move to improve income or opportunities and can usually return home. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Refer to the data below.

Table: forcibly displaced people worldwide (UNHCR, millions) - 2012: 45.2; 2017: 68.5; 2022: 108.4; mid-2024: 122.6.

Calculate the percentage increase between 2012 and mid-2024.
items.markingKey: (122.6 − 45.2)/45.2 × 100 = +171.2% Award 1 mark per valid point or correct step, up to [3]; data quoted must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

items.markingKey: (a) (122.6 − 45.2)/45.2 × 100 = +171.2% (b) A near tripling with acceleration after 2017 and 2022; new conflicts (Syria, Ukraine, Sudan, DR Congo) and protracted crises with few returns. items.stem: State what is meant by the term "brain gain".
items.answer: The benefit to a country from inflows of skilled migrants or the return of emigrants with new skills
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the benefit to a country from inflows of skilled migrants or the return of emigrants with new skills. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between the impacts on host countries and the impacts of migration on source countries.
items.answer: Source countries gain remittances but may lose young and skilled labour; host countries gain labour and taxes but may face pressure on services and social tensions.
items.markingKey: Source countries gain remittances but may lose young and skilled labour; host countries gain labour and taxes but may face pressure on services and social tensions. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Between 1990 and 2002 the population of a municipality on the edge of Nairobi changed from 288,114 to 476,650 people. Calculate the percentage change over the period.
items.markingKey: M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (476,650 − 288,114) ÷ 288,114 × 100; A1 +65.4% (sign or "increase/decrease" required).

items.stem:
Refer to the data below.

Table: remittances as % of GDP (World Bank, 2023) - Tajikistan 48; Tonga 41; Nepal 26; Philippines 9; Mexico 4; India 3.

Describe the pattern shown by the data.
items.answer: Small, low-income countries (Tajikistan, Tonga, Nepal) depend heavily on remittances; larger economies (Mexico, India) receive large totals that are small shares of GDP.
items.markingKey: Small, low-income countries (Tajikistan, Tonga, Nepal) depend heavily on remittances; larger economies (Mexico, India) receive large totals that are small shares of GDP. Award 1 mark per valid point or correct step, up to [3]; data quoted must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

items.stem:
Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

Bar chart description: remittances to India (US$ billion) - 2010: 53; 2015: 69; 2020: 83; 2023: 120.

(a) Calculate the percentage increase from 2010 to 2023. [4]
(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, suggest two reasons for the trend. [6]
items.answer: (a) (120 − 53)/53 × 100 = +126.4% (b) Growth of the Indian diaspora in the Gulf, USA and UK; higher-skilled migrants (IT, health) earning more; better digital transfer channels.
items.markingKey: (a) (120 − 53)/53 × 100 = +126.4% (b) Growth of the Indian diaspora in the Gulf, USA and UK; higher-skilled migrants (IT, health) earning more; better digital transfer channels. items.stem: Explain how host countries can benefit from international migration.
items.answer: Migrants fill labour shortages (care, construction, health), pay taxes, offset ageing and bring entrepreneurship and cultural diversity, e.g. Germany and Canada.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Migrants fill labour shortages (care, construction, health), pay taxes, offset ageing and bring entrepreneurship and cultural diversity, e.g. Germany and Canada. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Suggest two reasons why the Gulf states attract migrant workers from South Asia.
items.answer: High wages relative to home, labour demand in construction and services funded by oil wealth, recruitment agencies and established networks.
items.markingKey: High wages relative to home, labour demand in construction and services funded by oil wealth, recruitment agencies and established networks.

items.stem: "Remittances are the most important consequence of international migration for source countries." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Remittances are the most visible benefit, but demographic and social consequences can be equally important.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - arguments supporting the statement: larger than ODA and often FDI; reduce poverty directly. Arguments challenging it: loss of labour and skills, family separation and ageing; social and cultural change from return migrants. Evaluation should weigh places, scales, perspectives and time. Judgement: Remittances are the most visible benefit, but demographic and social consequences can be equally important. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A model showing how birth rates, death rates and population growth change through five stages as a country develops"?
items.answer: demographic transition model
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of demographic transition model.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "sex ratio"?
options: A model showing how birth rates, death rates and population growth change through five stages as a country develops
The emigration of highly educated or skilled people from their country of origin
The average number of children a woman would have during her reproductive years at current age-specific fertility rates
The number of males per 100 females in a population (or at birth)
items.answer: The number of males per 100 females in a population (or at birth)
items.markingKey: D. "sex ratio" is the number of males per 100 females in a population (or at birth).

items.stem: Which displacement crisis became the world's largest after war broke out in April 2023?
items.answer: Sudan
items.markingKey: Sudan. Over 10 million people were displaced inside and outside Sudan.

items.stem: A student claims: "International migrants mostly move from low-income to high-income countries." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Large flows are South-South (e.g. Burkina Faso to Côte d'Ivoire, Nepal to India, Bangladesh to the Gulf).
items.markingKey: Large flows are South-South (e.g. Burkina Faso to Côte d'Ivoire, Nepal to India, Bangladesh to the Gulf). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between stage 2 and stage 4 of the demographic transition model.
items.answer: In stage 2 death rates fall rapidly while birth rates remain high, so growth is rapid; in stage 4 both rates are low and growth is slow or stable.
items.markingKey: In stage 2 death rates fall rapidly while birth rates remain high, so growth is rapid; in stage 4 both rates are low and growth is slow or stable. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Population pyramids show only the effect of births and deaths." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: They also show migration (e.g. male bulge in the UAE), wars (missing cohorts in Russia) and past policies (China's one-child generation).
items.markingKey: They also show migration (e.g. male bulge in the UAE), wars (missing cohorts in Russia) and past policies (China's one-child generation). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Mei writes: "Most of the world's refugees live in Europe." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Around 70% live in countries neighbouring their own, and most are hosted by low- and middle-income countries such as Turkey, Iran, Colombia, Uganda and Pakistan.
items.markingKey: Around 70% live in countries neighbouring their own, and most are hosted by low- and middle-income countries such as Turkey, Iran, Colombia, Uganda and Pakistan. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why dependence on remittances can be risky for a source country.
items.answer: Flows depend on host-country economies and policies (e.g. Tajikistan's fall when Russia's economy weakened in 2014-15), may discourage local investment and labour, and can widen inequality between migrant and non-migrant households.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Flows depend on host-country economies and policies (e.g. Tajikistan's fall when Russia's economy weakened in 2014-15), may discourage local investment and labour, and can widen inequality between migrant and non-migrant households. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Falling death rates are mainly caused by better hospitals." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: In stage 2 the biggest gains come from clean water, sanitation, vaccination and better nutrition rather than hospital care.
items.markingKey: In stage 2 the biggest gains come from clean water, sanitation, vaccination and better nutrition rather than hospital care. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using Uganda as an example, explain the needs of a youthful population.
items.answer: Around 45% of the population is under 15 and the median age is about 16. Large cohorts require schools, health care and, soon, millions of new jobs.
items.markingKey: Context (Around 45% of the population is under 15 and the median age is about 16.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Large cohorts require schools, health care and, soon, millions of new jobs. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the needs of a youthful population.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Ukraine after February 2022 shows the role of host-country policy in shaping refugee outcomes.
items.answer: About 6 million refugees were recorded across Europe and millions more became IDPs. The EU Temporary Protection Directive gave immediate rights to work, housing and schooling.
items.markingKey: Context (About 6 million refugees were recorded across Europe and millions more became IDPs.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The EU Temporary Protection Directive gave immediate rights to work, housing and schooling. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the role of host-country policy in shaping refugee outcomes.

items.stem: With reference to Germany's 2015-16 asylum intake, explain how it illustrates host-country impacts of international migration.
items.answer: About 1.2 million asylum seekers arrived in 2015-16, many from Syria. Initial pressure on housing and integration services was followed by many entering the labour market and offsetting ageing.
items.markingKey: Context (About 1.2 million asylum seekers arrived in 2015-16, many from Syria.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Initial pressure on housing and integration services was followed by many entering the labour market and offsetting ageing. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to host-country impacts of international migration.

items.stem: A data table shows the number of births registered in a prefecture of Japan: 1995 - 4,578 births; 2015 - 10,002 births. Calculate the percentage change over the period.
items.markingKey: M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (10,002 − 4,578) ÷ 4,578 × 100; A1 +118.5% (sign or "increase/decrease" required).

Calculate the median, the interquartile range (quartiles as medians of the lower and upper halves) and the standard deviation (σ = √(Σ(x − x̄)²/n)).
items.markingKey: A1 median 237; M1 quartiles from ordered data (Q1 167, Q3 326); A1 IQR 159; M1 A1 σ = 94.26.

items.stem: Suggest two reasons why the number of forcibly displaced people has risen since 2012.
items.answer: New and continuing conflicts (Syria, South Sudan, Ukraine, Sudan, DR Congo), persecution (Rohingya), and fewer durable solutions such as return or resettlement.
items.markingKey: New and continuing conflicts (Syria, South Sudan, Ukraine, Sudan, DR Congo), persecution (Rohingya), and fewer durable solutions such as return or resettlement.

items.stem: Nepal received about US$10.9 billion in personal remittances in a year when its GDP was about US$39 billion. Calculate remittances as a percentage of GDP. Official development assistance (ODA) was US$1.7 billion: how many times larger were remittances? Explain one advantage of remittances over aid for households.
items.answer: 28.1% of GDP; 6.4 times ODA; remittances go directly to families (spent on food, schooling, housing) and are counter-cyclical.
items.markingKey: A1 28.1%; A1 6.4×; R1 R1 developed advantage.

items.stem: Examine the factors that cause fertility rates to vary between countries.
items.answer: Indicative content: Female education and employment, contraception, infant mortality, religion and culture, urbanisation, policy; contrasting examples (Niger vs South Korea, Kerala, Iran); judgement on most important factor.

items.stem:
Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

Description of a population pyramid for the United Arab Emirates: very narrow bars for 0-19 and 50+, but very wide male bars for ages 25-44, where males outnumber females by about three to one.

(a) Describe the pyramid. [4]
(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, explain the shape of the pyramid. [6]
items.answer: (a) Dominated by working-age adults, especially men aged 25-44; few children and elderly; highly unbalanced sex ratio. (b) Large-scale temporary male labour migration (construction, services) from South Asia under the kafala system; migrants rarely bring families or retire there.
items.markingKey: (a) Dominated by working-age adults, especially men aged 25-44; few children and elderly; highly unbalanced sex ratio. (b) Large-scale temporary male labour migration (construction, services) from South Asia under the kafala system; migrants rarely bring families or retire there. Credit relevant own knowledge and named examples in (b). Infographic markscheme [10]: part (a) [4] - award 1 mark per valid point taken from the resource (data must be quoted with units for full marks); part (b) [6] - up to 2 marks for each developed explanation linking the resource to own knowledge; reward named examples; maximum 3 marks if the resource is not used.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that the impacts of refugees on host countries are mainly negative?
items.answer: Impacts depend largely on host policies, international support and the scale and duration of displacement.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: pressure on services and infrastructure (Lebanon hosted about 1 refugee per 4-5 residents); environmental damage around camps (Cox's Bazar). Against / limitations: refugees bring labour and skills (Syrians in Turkish industry); Uganda's self-reliance policy allows refugees to farm and work, boosting local economies. A supported conclusion might be: Impacts depend largely on host policies, international support and the scale and duration of displacement. items.stem: To what extent do you agree that remittances are the most important consequence of international migration for source countries?
items.answer: Remittances are the most visible benefit, but demographic and social consequences can be equally important.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: larger than ODA and often FDI; reduce poverty directly. Against / limitations: loss of labour and skills, family separation and ageing; social and cultural change from return migrants. items.stem: Which country has one of the world's highest TFRs, at around 6?
items.answer: Niger
items.markingKey: A. Niger's TFR is about 6 children per woman, with a median age near 15.

items.stem: Define the term "youthful population".
items.answer: A population with a large proportion of children under 15, typically giving a wide-based pyramid
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a population with a large proportion of children under 15, typically giving a wide-based pyramid. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: According to UNHCR, approximately how many people were forcibly displaced worldwide by mid-2024?
items.answer: About 120 million
items.markingKey: A. UNHCR reported about 122.6 million forcibly displaced people in mid-2024, more than half of them IDPs.

items.stem: Mei writes: "Brain drain is always harmful to the source country." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Some source countries benefit from remittances, diaspora investment and return migration; the Philippines trains nurses partly for export.
items.markingKey: Some source countries benefit from remittances, diaspora investment and return migration; the Philippines trains nurses partly for export. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Falling death rates are mainly caused by better hospitals." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: In stage 2 the biggest gains come from clean water, sanitation, vaccination and better nutrition rather than hospital care.
items.markingKey: In stage 2 the biggest gains come from clean water, sanitation, vaccination and better nutrition rather than hospital care. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between an ageing population and a youthful population.
items.answer: A youthful population has a large share under 15 and a wide-based pyramid (e.g. Uganda); an ageing population has a growing share over 65 and a narrow base with wide upper bars (e.g. Italy).
items.markingKey: A youthful population has a large share under 15 and a wide-based pyramid (e.g. Uganda); an ageing population has a growing share over 65 and a narrow base with wide upper bars (e.g. Italy). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why protracted refugee situations develop.
items.answer: Conflicts continue for years (Syria, Afghanistan, Somalia), return is unsafe, local integration is restricted and resettlement places are few, so camps such as Dadaab (Kenya, since 1991) become semi-permanent.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Conflicts continue for years (Syria, Afghanistan, Somalia), return is unsafe, local integration is restricted and resettlement places are few, so camps such as Dadaab (Kenya, since 1991) become semi-permanent. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between brain drain and brain circulation.
items.answer: Brain drain is the permanent loss of skilled people from a source country; brain circulation is the flow of skilled migrants back and forth, bringing skills, capital and networks home (e.g. Indian IT professionals returning to Bengaluru).
items.markingKey: Brain drain is the permanent loss of skilled people from a source country; brain circulation is the flow of skilled migrants back and forth, bringing skills, capital and networks home (e.g. Indian IT professionals returning to Bengaluru). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why the DTM may not predict the future population change of low-income countries accurately.
items.answer: It is based on the experience of western Europe; transitions in Asia have been faster, some African countries' fertility decline has stalled, and the model ignores migration, HIV/AIDS, policies and globalisation.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It is based on the experience of western Europe; transitions in Asia have been faster, some African countries' fertility decline has stalled, and the model ignores migration, HIV/AIDS, policies and globalisation. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Census data for a prefecture in rural Japan: aged 0-14: 13,000; aged 15-64: 111,000; aged 65 and over: 36,000. Calculate the total dependency ratio.
items.markingKey: M1 (young + old) ÷ working-age × 100; A1 44.1 dependants per 100 people of working age.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Rohingya crisis of 2017 and explain what it reveals about the causes and impacts of forced migration.
items.answer: Over 700,000 Rohingya fled Myanmar's Rakhine State to Bangladesh in 2017 after military violence. Ethnic persecution caused mass flight, and the influx strained the environment and services of Cox's Bazar district.
items.markingKey: Context (Over 700,000 Rohingya fled Myanmar's Rakhine State to Bangladesh in 2017 after military violence.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Ethnic persecution caused mass flight, and the influx strained the environment and services of Cox's Bazar district. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the causes and impacts of forced migration.

items.stem: The UAE (population 10 million) has a natural increase of 10.9 per 1,000. In one year it received 755 thousand immigrants and 256 thousand people emigrated. Calculate the net migration rate and the overall rate of population change per 1,000, and state which component dominates.
items.answer: net migration +49.9 per 1,000; total change +60.8 per 1,000; dominant component: migration
items.markingKey: A1 +49.9; M1 natural change + net migration; A1 +60.8; R1 migration.

items.stem: Estimates for Brazil give a crude birth rate (CBR) of 13.3 per 1,000 and a crude death rate (CDR) of 6.8 per 1,000. Calculate (i) the rate of natural increase as a percentage and (ii) the doubling time, using the rule of 70.
Between 1995 and 2010 the number of international migrants living in a London borough changed from 83,238 to 109,612 people. Calculate the percentage change over the period.
items.markingKey: M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (109,612 − 83,238) ÷ 83,238 × 100; A1 +31.7% (sign or "increase/decrease" required).

items.stem: Nepal (population 30 million) has a natural increase of 10.5 per 1,000. In one year it received 25 thousand immigrants and 486 thousand people emigrated. Calculate the net migration rate and the overall rate of population change per 1,000, and state which component dominates.
items.answer: net migration -15.4 per 1,000; total change -4.9 per 1,000; dominant component: migration
items.markingKey: A1 -15.4; M1 natural change + net migration; A1 -4.9; R1 migration.

items.stem:
Refer to the data below.

Bar chart description: remittances to India (US$ billion) - 2010: 53; 2015: 69; 2020: 83; 2023: 120.

Suggest two reasons for the trend.
items.answer: Growth of the Indian diaspora in the Gulf, USA and UK; higher-skilled migrants (IT, health) earning more; better digital transfer channels.
items.markingKey: Growth of the Indian diaspora in the Gulf, USA and UK; higher-skilled migrants (IT, health) earning more; better digital transfer channels. Award 1 mark per valid point or correct step, up to [3]; data quoted must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

items.stem:
Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

Table: CBR and CDR (per 1,000) for four countries - Niger 44, 9; India 16, 7; Brazil 12, 7; Japan 6, 13.

(a) Calculate the natural increase rate (%) for each country. [4]
(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, assign each country to a DTM stage, justifying with the data. [6]
items.answer: (a) Niger 3.5%; India 0.9%; Brazil 0.5%; Japan −0.7% (natural decrease). (b) Niger stage 2 (high CBR, low CDR); India late stage 3 (falling CBR); Brazil stage 3-4 (low rates, slow growth); Japan stage 5 (CDR > CBR).

items.stem: To what extent is it true that the dependency ratio is a reliable indicator of the economic burden on the working population? Refer to places and scales you have studied.
items.answer: It is a useful but crude indicator that should be combined with labour participation data.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - arguments supporting the statement: simple, comparable across countries; signals future pension and education demand. Arguments challenging it: ignores working elderly and non-working adults; ignores productivity, unemployment and informal work. Evaluation should weigh places, scales, perspectives and time.
